title: Data Contracts, Lineage & Semantic Consistency
interviewAnswer: Data contracts make schemas, ownership and expectations explicit; lineage shows downstream dependencies. Together they reduce silent breakage and clarify impact when producers change data.
keyPoints: Schema compatibility is not enough; semantics matter.
Owners and SLAs should be explicit.
why: Data Contracts, Lineage & Semantic Consistency appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.
intuition: Schema compatibility is not enough; semantics matter.
deepDive: Data contracts make schemas, ownership and expectations explicit; lineage shows downstream dependencies. Together they reduce silent breakage and clarify impact when producers change data. Owners and SLAs should be explicit. Metric definitions should be centralized/versioned. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.
workedExample: Changing “revenue” from gross to net without versioning can silently corrupt every downstream dashboard/model.
commonMistakes: Applying the method without checking its assumptions or data-generating process.
Choosing it because it is familiar rather than comparing against an appropriate baseline.
followUps: What assumptions does Data Contracts, Lineage & Semantic Consistency make?
How would you validate or debug Data Contracts, Lineage & Semantic Consistency in practice?
production: In production, validate assumptions on real data, monitor the quantities that can drift, and keep a simple baseline so added complexity has a measurable reason to exist.
